The INP‐ABM program will enable students to complete a bachelor and master’s program in a five-year period.
Because of the proposed structure of the ABM program, the cost incurred by the student will be substantially less than the traditional path of completing a 4-year bachelor’s degree followed by a 2-year master’s program.

This program will also provide students with the opportunity to enter the neuroscience workforce with all the benefits of a master’s degree without losing the time and expenses that two years of traditional graduate study would otherwise cost them.
As noted previously, students will complete the same graduate level course work on the INP Master’s, non-thesis or thesis track, thereby becoming knowledgeable about general neuroscience topics as well as research methods, neurobiology, neuroethics, human neuroanatomy and neurology, and much more.

The goal of the program is for students to be able complete an accelerated bachelor to masters program within a five-year period.

The INP ABM program aligns with the University’s mission and strategic plan by supporting the University’s quest for knowledge and serving and enriching the lives of its students.
The key players in the INP ABM program, namely the students, faculty, staff, will be striving to achieve one common purpose: to learn and lead together.
The ABM program also aligns with the current strategic plan by fostering student success, exposing students to cutting edge research and lab techniques, and by embracing diversity at both the student and faculty level.
It is important to note that the INP is committed to supporting the diversity of the neuroscience students and has a Standing Committee, the Diversity Initiative Committee, devoted to this effort.
Recent research regarding graduation trends in neuroscience supports that greater numbers of females are graduating from neuroscience bachelor’s and graduate degree programs.
White (non-Hispanic) males and females represent the largest group of graduates and Asian/Pacific Islanders represent the largest non-White group of graduates.

These findings support that although the number of underrepresented minorities graduating from neuroscience degree programs at every level has increased in recent years, they are still fewer in number compared to White (non-Hispanic) and Asian/Pacific Islanders (Ramos et al., 2017).

CONSTITUTION, BY-LAWS, AND UNIVERSITY MANUAL COMMITTEEReport #2022-2023-15 - SECOND READING OF MOTION TO AMEND THE SENATE BY-LAWSFACULTY SENATE, March 23, 2023 Background and contextIn response to the discussion about preferred modalities of Faculty Senate meetings that arose duringthe Senate meeting on October 20, 2022 and that was included as “Old Business” in the agenda forthe Senate meeting on November 17, 2022, CBUM discussed the issue and with the agenda for theFaculty Senate meeting on December 8, 2022 included for consideration a report with a motion toamend the By-Laws of the Faculty Senate to continue to permit the option of remote participation inFaculty Senate meetings.
During the December 8, 2022 meeting, prior to the presentation of theCBUM report, Senator Preisser moved to eliminate the possibility of remote participation in FacultySenate meetings.
The motion failed.
Subsequently Senate Vice President Nassersharif moved to tablethe CBUM motion to codify the option of remote participation in in-person Senate meetings in theFaculty Senate By-Laws.
A majority of the Senate voted in favor of Vice President Nassersharif’smotion.

In January 2023 CBUM revised the original motion and submitted a new version to FSEC whorequested that the committee draft specific language changes to the By-Laws for consideration by theFaculty Senate.
RationaleIn recognition of the critical role of meaningful faculty engagement in shared governance, CBUMaffirms that it is essential that Faculty Senators, ex officio members of the Faculty Senate, andmembers of the General Faculty actively participate in Faculty Senate deliberations and meetings.
Thecommittee further urges that all members of the university community participate in Faculty Senatemeetings in-person whenever possible, as a matter of cohesion and of maximizing opportunities tosupport and nurture our sense of community.

Although the committee urges in-person attendanceand participation whenever possible, in the interests of equity and inclusion and as a means tooptimize our democratic processes by facilitating the broadest level possible of engagement withFaculty Senate business and participation in Faculty Senate deliberations, CBUM invites the FacultySenate to consider amending the By-Laws to codify the option for remote attendance for all in-personFaculty Senate meetings, with community members, Senators, and ex officio members who attendvirtually retaining all rights afforded to people who are able to attend in-person:- All attendees retain the right to speak and to participate in discussions.- All ex officio members of the Faculty Senate retain the right to make and second motions.- All Senators retain the right to make and second motions, and to vote.
Current language in the By-Laws of the Faculty Senate: 7.3 Regular Faculty Senate Meetings shall be held at least once each month on Thursdays during the academic year.
Proposed changes: 7.3 Regular Faculty Senate Meetings shall be held at least once each month on Thursdays during the academic year.

To facilitate the broadest level possible of engagement with Faculty Senate business, all in-person Faculty Senate meetings shall include an option for remote attendance, with community members, Senators, and ex officio members attending remotely retaining the same rights they enjoy when attending in-person and when attending fully virtual meetings.
